## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Jambukajātaka* (Ja 335) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya. The framing story recounts that the Buddha delivered this tale while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) near Rājagaha, occasioned by Devadatta's attempt to imitate the Buddha (*Sugatālayakaraṇa*) [Fausböll 1883]. In the narrative of the past, a jackal lives on the leftover prey provided by a lion (the Bodhisatta) [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. Growing arrogant, the jackal decides to act like a lion himself and, ignoring all advice, attacks an elephant, only to be killed on the spot [Anandajoti 2010]. At the conclusion of the story (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the jackal as Devadatta and the lion as himself [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883].

In modern anthologies and listings, the tale is cited as an illustration of the moral principle of "knowing one's strengths" through the foolish mimicry of the powerful [Anandajoti 2010]. The text's opening verse begins with *Brahā pavaddhakāyo so* [Fausböll 1883].

 Within the Pali tradition, machine analysis via DharmaNexus indicates five textual matches (685 characters) sharing substantial segments with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Volume 3), specifically between segments 2.1–4.4 of the canonical text and sections 908–915 of the commentary [DharmaNexus].
